case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Title VII requires an employee challenging a discriminatory job transfer to prove a materially significant disadvantage (beyond discrimination affecting “terms, conditions, or privileges” of employment), or whether any nontrivial discriminatory change in the terms or conditions of employment is actionable even without changes to pay or rank.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1) (prohibiting discrimination with respect to an individual’s “compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that the Eighth Circuit applied an improperly heightened “materially significant disadvantage” standard that is not found in Title VII’s text; she contends that a discriminatory transfer that alters the terms or conditions of employment (even without pay or rank loss) can violate Title VII, and that requiring a heightened harm threshold improperly shields discriminatory job reassignments from liability.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that petitioner’s transfer is not actionable because it caused no objective, material employment harm—no change in pay, rank, or supervisory status—and her claims of diminished prestige or increased administrative duties were conclusory and contradicted by the summary-judgment record; they also contend she forfeited certain arguments about altered conditions (schedule/attire/geography/vehicle), and that some alleged changes stemmed from the FBI’s revocation of her TFO status rather than the City’s transfer decision, which the lower courts found not attributable to the City.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito is right that we need an objective limiting principle to keep Title VII from becoming a super-personnel code, but his proposed “materially significant disadvantage” screen risks adding an atextual hurdle that narrows “terms, conditions, or privileges of employment” to something like pay-or-rank loss. As Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett emphasize, the statute’s own words already do the limiting work: only nontrivial, objectively identifiable changes in duties, schedule, or working conditions qualify, while mere subjective preferences and trivial slights do not. Justice Kavanaugh’s citation to Morgan matters because it confirms transfers are treated as discrete acts potentially actionable under Title VII, which counsels against a categorical rule that lateral transfers are generally nonactionable absent pay or title reduction. And I agree with Justice Gorsuch that Ellerth’s “tangible employment action” framework is a vicarious-liability tool in harassment doctrine and should not be converted into a substantive narrowing of § 2000e-2(a)(1).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability concern is serious, but his “material employment disadvantage” screen is not rooted in the enacted words; § 2000e-2(a)(1) already limits liability to discrimination "with respect to" compensation or the "terms, conditions, or privileges of employment," which in ordinary usage excludes trivial slights yet reaches real changes in duties, schedules, or workplace environment. As the Chief Justice notes, Ellerth’s “tangible employment action” arose to allocate vicarious liability in harassment cases and cannot be repurposed to narrow the substantive prohibition Congress wrote. Justice Kavanaugh’s invocation of Morgan, while about timeliness, reinforces that transfer decisions are the kind of employer acts Title VII contemplates; the remaining question is simply whether the transfer affected a term or condition of employment, not whether it cleared an atextual “significant disadvantage” hurdle. Under a textualist and originalist approach, we should reverse the Eighth Circuit’s heightened standard and apply the statute’s objective, workplace-anchored language.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right that we should not graft pay-or-rank loss onto § 2000e-2(a)(1), and I accept their point that “terms, conditions, or privileges” can include changes in duties or schedules. But their “nontrivial change” formulation does not supply a sufficiently objective, administrable limit and risks inviting courts to police ordinary staffing and assignment decisions—especially in law-enforcement contexts—based on amorphous notions of “prestige” or workplace preference. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Morgan does not move me because Morgan’s “discrete acts” discussion addressed timeliness, not the substantive threshold for what counts as discrimination with respect to employment “terms” or “conditions.” Absent a clearer, text-anchored showing of an objectively identifiable workplace detriment on this record, I continue to think the Eighth Circuit’s material-disadvantage screen best prevents Title VII from becoming a super-personnel code without rewriting the statute into an anything-goes standard.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability concern is real, but his proposed “material disadvantage” screen is not compelled by § 2000e-2(a)(1) and would, in practice, immunize discriminatory reassignments that worsen schedules, duties, safety, or family stability without changing pay or title—harms that fall most heavily on workers with the least power to refuse. As Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, the statute’s own limiter—discrimination “with respect to” the “terms, conditions, or privileges of employment”—already excludes trivial slights while capturing objectively verifiable changes in day-to-day working conditions; courts can apply that without becoming super-personnel departments. Justice Kavanaugh’s point about Morgan usefully reinforces that transfer decisions are treated as discrete acts in Title VII’s framework, supporting that the question is the character of the change in working conditions, not whether it crosses an extra-textual “significance” threshold. And I agree with Justice Gorsuch that Ellerth’s “tangible employment action” is a vicarious-liability construct in harassment doctrine, not a basis to narrow the substantive discrimination prohibition beyond Congress’s text.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability concern is the best point for the respondent, but his proposed “materially significant disadvantage” screen is not textually moored and risks collapsing “terms, conditions, or privileges” into a pay/title/status test Congress did not enact. As the Chief Justice notes, the statute itself supplies an objective limit: a transfer is actionable only if it nontrivially alters the employee’s actual work conditions (duties, schedule, location, safety, or similar objective features), which keeps courts out of mere preference disputes without adding extra-statutory hurdles. Justice Kavanaugh’s invocation of Morgan usefully confirms that transfers are treated as discrete acts capable of being unlawful; while Morgan is a timeliness case, it undercuts any instinct to treat lateral transfers as categorically outside § 2000e-2(a)(1). And I agree with Justice Gorsuch that Ellerth’s “tangible employment action” is a vicarious-liability tool in harassment doctrine, not a substantive definition that can narrow the discrimination text here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability concern is serious, but his proposed “materially significant disadvantage” screen still lacks a textual foothold and risks collapsing “terms, conditions, or privileges of employment” into a pay/title proxy Congress did not enact. As Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice note, § 2000e-2(a)(1) already contains an objective limit: the challenged action must be “with respect to” identifiable employment “terms” or “conditions,” which naturally excludes mere slights or purely subjective prestige complaints. Justice Kavanaugh’s reference to Morgan is helpful insofar as it confirms transfers are the kind of discrete employment actions Title VII routinely addresses, even if Morgan’s holding was about timeliness rather than the substantive threshold. And I agree with Justice Barrett that Ellerth’s “tangible employment action” framework, developed for vicarious liability in harassment cases, cannot be transmuted into a substantive narrowing of the discrimination ban without rewriting the statute.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability concern is serious, but his proposed “materially significant disadvantage” screen is not anchored in the enacted words and risks narrowing § 2000e-2(a)(1) to pay-or-rank harms Congress did not specify. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, the statute itself supplies the limiting principle—only nontrivial, objective changes in the “terms, conditions, or privileges of employment” qualify—so courts can filter out petty slights without importing Ellerth’s “tangible employment action,” which arose in a distinct vicarious-liability setting. Alito is right that Morgan did not decide the substantive threshold, but Morgan’s treatment of transfers as “discrete acts” supports that transfers can be actionable when they meaningfully alter job conditions rather than being categorically insulated absent pay/title loss. On an institutionalist view, adopting a text-based “real, nontrivial change” standard best aligns with precedent, preserves administrability, and avoids rewriting Title VII.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability concern is the strongest counterargument, but it does not justify adding a free‑standing “materially significant disadvantage” requirement absent in §2000e‑2(a)(1); the enacted text already limits liability to discrimination “with respect to” objectively ascertainable “terms, conditions, or privileges of employment.” As the Chief Justice notes, a “nontrivial change” requirement can do the needed work without collapsing the statute into a pay-or-title test, and it better tracks the ordinary meaning of “terms” and “conditions.” Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Morgan reinforces that transfer decisions are treated as discrete employment actions; while Morgan is not itself a threshold-of-harm case, it undercuts any suggestion that transfers are presumptively outside Title VII unless accompanied by economic loss. Finally, I agree with Justice Gorsuch that Ellerth’s “tangible employment action” is a vicarious-liability concept and cannot be repurposed to narrow the substantive prohibition Congress wrote.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability concern is serious, but I do not see it as a reason to graft a pay/title-centric “materially significant disadvantage” screen onto § 2000e-2(a)(1); the statute already limits actionable conduct to discrimination “with respect to” the employee’s objectively identifiable “terms, conditions, or privileges of employment,” which permits courts to dismiss trivial slights while reaching concrete changes in schedules, duties, safety, or training opportunities. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Ellerth’s “tangible employment action” was crafted for vicarious-liability allocation in harassment cases and should not be repurposed to narrow the substantive reach of the discrimination provision. Justice Kavanaugh’s point about Morgan—that transfer-related decisions are treated as discrete acts—supports that transfers can be actionable when they nontrivially alter workplace conditions, even if Morgan does not itself define the threshold. Under a pragmatic, fairness-focused approach, an atextual heightened-harm rule risks systematically under-remedying discriminatory reassignments that predictably worsen day-to-day working life while leaving formal rank or pay untouched.

John Roberts.reasoning: Title VII’s text makes it unlawful to discriminate with respect to an employee’s “compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), and a job transfer can alter those terms and conditions even absent a reduction in pay or rank. The Court should avoid importing atextual, heightened requirements like a “materially significant disadvantage” threshold that risks insulating discriminatory reassignment decisions from liability and creating unnecessary circuit variation. Burlington Industries, Inc. v. Ellerth addressed vicarious-liability rules in supervisor-harassment cases and the distinct concept of “tangible employment action,” not the substantive scope of § 2000e-2(a)(1); it therefore does not compel a categorical “material harm” prerequisite for discriminatory transfers. A narrow ruling can recognize that an actionable transfer must bring about a nontrivial change in terms or conditions of employment, while leaving case-specific disputes about forfeiture and causation to the lower courts on remand.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of Title VII makes it unlawful to “discriminate against any individual with respect to his compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), and nothing in that language imposes an extra-statutory requirement that the employee prove a “materially significant disadvantage” such as a pay or rank reduction. Under the ordinary public meaning of “terms” and “conditions” in 1964, a discriminatory transfer that nontrivially alters an employee’s work assignments, schedule, duties, or workplace conditions qualifies as discrimination “with respect to” those terms or conditions, even if it is a lateral move. Our precedents confirm that Title VII’s coverage extends beyond wages and formal title and reaches employment opportunities and conditions more generally. Because the Eighth Circuit’s heightened standard lacks a textual basis and risks insulating discriminatory reassignment decisions, I would reverse.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 2000e-2(a)(1) forbids discrimination with respect to an employee’s “compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment,” and that language is best read to require an objective change in the employment relationship—not merely a nontrivial, subjective dissatisfaction with a reassignment. Unlike Title VII’s retaliation provision, which this Court construed broadly in Burlington N. & Santa Fe Ry. Co. v. White, 548 U.S. 53, 66 (2006), the discrimination provision is anchored to workplace “terms” and “conditions,” supporting a limiting principle that screens out routine personnel moves unless they impose a material employment disadvantage. Requiring such a threshold also avoids turning federal courts into super-personnel departments second-guessing day-to-day law-enforcement staffing decisions, a practical consequence Congress did not clearly command in the text. On this record—no change in pay or rank and only conclusory claims of diminished prestige—the Eighth Circuit’s material-disadvantage approach appropriately enforces Title VII without expanding it beyond its traditional boundaries.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Title VII’s text makes it unlawful to discriminate with respect to an individual’s “compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), and it does not add a judicially created requirement that the employee show a “materially significant disadvantage” beyond a nontrivial discriminatory change in those terms or conditions. Burlington Northern & Santa Fe Ry. Co. v. White, 548 U.S. 53 (2006), adopted a “materially adverse” standard only for retaliation under § 2000e-3(a) because that provision is not limited to workplace terms and conditions, so its limiting principle should not be imported into the substantive antidiscrimination provision. Requiring a heightened harm threshold would insulate discriminatory reassignments that concretely worsen day-to-day working conditions (even without pay or rank loss), undercutting Title VII’s remedial purpose and disproportionately harming workers with less power to resist biased transfers. The proper rule is that a discriminatory transfer is actionable when it causes a real, nontrivial change in the employee’s “terms, conditions, or privileges” of employment, with disputes about the extent and cause of particular harms resolved on the record rather than by an extra-textual categorical bar.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Title VII’s disparate-treatment provision makes it unlawful to discriminate with respect to an individual’s “compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), and that text already supplies the limiting principle: the challenged action must nontrivially affect the employee’s terms or conditions. Importing a further judicially created “materially significant disadvantage” requirement risks rewriting the statute and would improperly borrow from the retaliation context, where Burlington Northern & Santa Fe Ry. Co. v. White adopted a “materially adverse” standard precisely because § 2000e-3(a) is not limited to employment “terms” and “conditions.” A workable middle-ground reading is that purely trivial slights are not actionable, but a discriminatory transfer that meaningfully changes duties, schedule, or other conditions can be, even absent pay or rank loss. On this view, the Eighth Circuit’s heightened harm standard is inconsistent with § 2000e-2(a)(1)’s text and structure, though the plaintiff must still prove a real (not speculative) change in conditions attributable to the employer.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Title VII makes it unlawful to discriminate “with respect to … compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), and that text contains no extra requirement that the employee also show a “materially significant disadvantage” beyond a nontrivial discriminatory change in those terms or conditions. Reading such a heightened harm threshold into the statute risks adding words Congress did not enact and would improperly narrow liability for discriminatory reassignments that alter duties or working conditions even without changes to pay or rank. Ellerth’s “tangible employment action” formulation arose in a distinct vicarious-liability framework for supervisor harassment and, as Burlington N. & Santa Fe Ry. Co. v. White explains, Ellerth did not purport to define the substantive scope of § 2000e-2(a)(1). The proper rule, faithful to the statute’s plain meaning and separation-of-powers principles, is that discriminatory transfers affecting the terms, conditions, or privileges of employment are actionable without an atextual “significant disadvantage” overlay.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Title VII’s text makes it unlawful to discriminate with respect to an employee’s “compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), and does not impose an extra-textual requirement that the employee show a “materially significant disadvantage” akin to an economic-loss threshold. This Court has recognized that Title VII reaches discrimination affecting workplace conditions even absent direct pay or rank consequences, including in the harassment framework where liability can attach without a separate showing of “objectively tangible” economic harm. In National Railroad Passenger Corp. v. Morgan, we identified “denial of transfer” as a discrete act that is separately actionable under Title VII, which undercuts a rule that most discriminatory transfers are nonactionable unless they produce a substantial, independently “material” detriment. Practical administrability is served by requiring a nontrivial change in terms or conditions caused by discrimination—while leaving factbound disputes (including forfeiture and causation questions about which changes are attributable to the employer) to be resolved on remand under the correct legal standard.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Title VII makes it unlawful to discriminate with respect to an individual’s “compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), and that text contains no freestanding requirement that the plaintiff show a “materially significant disadvantage” beyond a nontrivial discriminatory change in those terms or conditions. Importing a heightened harm threshold risks rewriting the statute to focus only on economic or status-based injury, contrary to this Court’s recognition that Title VII reaches more than strictly “economic” discrimination. Burlington Industries, Inc. v. Ellerth defined “tangible employment action” for purposes of vicarious liability in harassment cases and did not purport to narrow the scope of § 2000e-2(a)(1)’s substantive prohibition on discrimination in “terms” and “conditions.” Consistent with text and methodological discipline, the proper inquiry is whether the challenged transfer imposed a nontrivial discriminatory change in the terms or conditions of employment, not whether it also produced a materially significant disadvantage in pay or rank.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Title VII’s text makes it unlawful to discriminate with respect to an employee’s “compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), and nothing in that language imposes an extra requirement that the plaintiff show a “materially significant disadvantage” such as a pay or rank cut. This Court has emphasized that Title VII is not limited to purely economic harms and instead reaches the “entire spectrum of disparate treatment” in the workplace, including discriminatory alterations of working conditions. Burlington Industries, Inc. v. Ellerth addressed vicarious liability in supervisor-harassment cases and the meaning of “tangible employment action,” not the threshold for what discriminatory actions are covered by § 2000e-2(a)(1), and Burlington N. & Santa Fe Ry. Co. v. White underscores that Ellerth does not define the scope of the general antidiscrimination provision. A rule requiring a heightened adversity showing would, as a practical matter, permit discriminatory reassignments that meaningfully worsen work conditions so long as pay and title remain constant, undermining Title VII’s core guarantee of equal treatment at work.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Title VII requires a plaintiff challenging a discriminatory job transfer to show a materially significant employment disadvantage (beyond discrimination in the "terms, conditions, or privileges" of employment) to establish an actionable adverse employment action.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1) (prohibiting discrimination with respect to an individual’s “compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment” because of a protected characteristic).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that the Eighth Circuit applied an improperly restrictive standard by requiring an employee challenging a discriminatory transfer to show a significant, material employment disadvantage (often framed as tangible harm like reduced pay or rank). She contends Title VII’s text covers discriminatory changes to “terms” and “conditions” of employment even when pay and formal title remain the same, and that forcing a heightened harm requirement narrows Title VII beyond what Congress enacted and creates an unjustified circuit split.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that a purely lateral transfer with no change in pay, rank, or supervisory authority is not actionable under Title VII absent objective, material harm. They emphasize petitioner’s record concessions that her transfer caused no pay/rank/supervisory change and did not harm career prospects, and they characterize her claims of lost prestige or increased administrative work as conclusory and unsupported. They also contend certain asserted negative changes were forfeited or are attributable to the FBI’s revocation of her TFO status rather than the City’s transfer decision, and thus cannot supply the required harm attributable to the employer.
key_precedents: No specific Supreme Court precedents are quoted or clearly identified by name in the provided excerpts; the dispute is framed primarily around the interpretation of Title VII’s “terms, conditions, or privileges” language and an asserted circuit split over the required level of harm for transfer claims.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s workability point remains the strongest counterargument, and we should meet it by requiring an objective, concrete disadvantageous change in the employee’s “terms, conditions, or privileges of employment,” not merely a subjective preference or wounded pride. But I agree with Justices Kagan and Gorsuch that importing Burlington Northern’s “materially adverse” retaliation screen would be a mismatch to § 2000e-2(a)(1)’s text, which is already workplace-tethered, and with Justice Kavanaugh that Ellerth’s “tangible employment action” concept arose in a vicarious-liability framework rather than defining § 703(a)(1)’s substantive scope. Morgan’s identification of a “transfer” as a discrete act for limitations purposes does not answer the merits question, but it reinforces that we can treat transfers as potentially actionable while still insisting the plaintiff show a real alteration in employment conditions. A narrow holding on the statute’s own terms preserves administrability and institutional legitimacy without adopting an atextual “materially significant disadvantage” gloss.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is the administrability concern, but under a textualist and original-public-meaning approach we cannot add an extra-statutory “materially significant disadvantage” requirement that Congress did not enact in § 2000e-2(a)(1). As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch explain, the statute already limits actionable discrimination to changes “with respect to … compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment,” which permits courts to reject mere slights or subjective dissatisfaction without inventing a new severity threshold. Justice Alito’s reliance on Burlington Northern is unpersuasive because, as Justice Kagan notes, that “materially adverse” standard was tailored to § 2000e-3(a)’s different text, and importing it here would collapse Congress’s distinct wording choices. Morgan’s identification of “transfer” as a discrete act does not itself set a harm threshold, and Ellerth’s “tangible employment action” framework concerns vicarious liability rather than redefining the substantive scope of § 703(a)(1).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I accept Chief Justice Roberts’s point that Burlington Northern’s “materially adverse” formulation cannot simply be transplanted into §2000e-2(a)(1) given the different statutory text, and I would not rest my view on that label. But Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch’s response still leaves, in my view, the central textual problem: “terms, conditions, or privileges of employment” implies an objective, employment-relevant alteration, and not every lateral reassignment that an employee prefers less qualifies as a change in those terms or conditions. Justice Thomas is right that duties and schedules can be “terms” or “conditions,” yet that does not answer whether a transfer with no concrete diminution (pay, rank, benefits, materially worse duties or hours) is actionable; Morgan’s “discrete act” point speaks to timeliness, not to the requisite level of employment impact. Because the petitioners’ approach risks drawing courts into routine supervisory decisions on thin showings of harm, I would adhere to a rule requiring a real, nontrivial change in employment conditions, closer to the Eighth Circuit’s understanding, while clarifying it must be grounded in the statutory terms rather than retaliation doctrine.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is the administrability concern—without a harm threshold, Title VII could become a vehicle for ordinary assignment disputes—but the statute itself supplies the limiting principle: the challenged action must discriminate “with respect to … terms, conditions, or privileges of employment,” which already excludes trivial slights while covering real changes in duties, safety, schedule, or professional standing that often most burden vulnerable workers. Burlington Northern v. White does not support importing a “materially adverse” screen into § 2000e-2(a)(1) because, as Justice Kagan explains, White’s standard was tied to retaliation’s broader statutory language, not discrimination’s workplace-tethered text. Justice Roberts’s concern about judge-made, circuit-varying “significant disadvantage” tests reinforces that the Eighth Circuit’s gloss risks narrowing Congress’s protections in precisely the contexts where discriminatory transfers are used as a tool of exclusion. I would hold that a discriminatory transfer is actionable when it meaningfully alters a term or condition of employment, without demanding an additional, atextual showing of “materially significant” harm beyond the discriminatory change itself.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s workability point is the best argument for the respondent, but I don’t think it justifies importing an extra-statutory “materially significant disadvantage” requirement: the text already limits actionable discrimination to acts taken “with respect to … compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment,” which screens out mere workplace slights. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Burlington Northern’s “materially adverse” framework was a tailored response to § 2000e-3(a)’s broader retaliation language; transplanting it here would collapse Congress’s structural distinction between discrimination and retaliation provisions. Alito’s additional reliance on Ellerth’s “tangible employment action” concept remains a mismatch (as Justice Kavanaugh notes) because it addressed vicarious liability and defenses in harassment cases, not the substantive reach of § 703(a)(1). The administrable middle ground is to require a concrete, nontrivial change that qualifies as a term/condition of employment—without adding a free-floating “significant harm” gloss that narrows the statute beyond its words.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point remains workability—courts should not become super-personnel departments for every disliked reassignment—but that concern must be handled within the statute Congress wrote, not by importing an extra-statutory “materially significant disadvantage” threshold. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 2000e-2(a)(1) already cabins liability to discrimination “with respect to … compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment,” which permits courts to require an objective, concrete change to those terms or conditions while still rejecting claims based on mere bruised ego. Burlington Northern v. White cannot do the heavy lifting Alito wants because its “material adversity” standard was tailored to § 2000e-3(a)’s broader retaliation text, and Justice Kavanaugh is right that Ellerth’s “tangible employment action” framework was designed for vicarious-liability doctrine, not to redefine § 703(a)(1)’s substantive scope. On a textualist/originalist approach, the Eighth Circuit’s heightened gloss risks narrowing Title VII beyond its public meaning; close line-drawing should be left to applying “terms” and “conditions” to the facts, not rewriting the statute.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s administrability point remains the best argument for the Respondent, but it does not justify importing Burlington Northern’s retaliation-specific “materially adverse” threshold into § 2000e-2(a)(1), as the Chief Justice explains, because the discrimination provision is already textually confined to “compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment.” I agree with Justice Roberts that the workable limiting principle is to require an objectively disadvantageous change that meaningfully alters an employment term or condition—more than hurt feelings, but not an atextual “materially significant disadvantage” prerequisite. Alito’s additional reliance on Ellerth’s “tangible employment action” framework does not move me because, as I noted and Justice Kagan reinforced, that doctrine arose in the vicarious-liability/affirmative-defense setting for harassment and should not be used to narrow the substantive scope of § 703(a)(1). On remand, close cases can be handled through ordinary application of “terms and conditions,” causation, and summary-judgment standards without creating a new, judge-made severity screen.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s workability concern is the strongest point for the respondent, but on a textualist account we cannot add an extra “materially significant disadvantage” prerequisite when Congress already limited liability to discrimination “with respect to … compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, that language supplies an objective limiting principle—requiring a concrete, nontrivial alteration to employment terms or conditions—without importing Burlington Northern’s retaliation-specific “materially adverse” standard keyed to different statutory text. Justice Alito’s reliance on Ellerth’s “tangible employment action” does not persuade me because, as Justice Kavanaugh notes, it was crafted for vicarious-liability/affirmative-defense doctrine in harassment cases and should not be repurposed to narrow § 2000e-2(a)(1)’s substantive reach. Morgan’s characterization of transfers as discrete acts (even if directed to timeliness) reinforces that transfers are within the statute’s domain, leaving the remaining line-drawing to whether the transfer actually changed a term or condition of employment under ordinary meaning rather than atextual severity gloss.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s workability concern is the strongest counterweight, but I do not think it justifies layering an atextual “materially significant disadvantage” requirement on top of § 2000e-2(a)(1), which already cabins liability to discrimination “with respect to … compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment.” As Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the proper limiting principle is to require a concrete, employment-relevant alteration in those terms or conditions—enough to screen out mere slights—without importing Burlington Northern’s retaliation-specific “materially adverse” test that responded to different statutory language. Alito’s reliance on Ellerth’s “tangible employment action” likewise does not move me because, as Justice Kavanaugh explains, that concept was crafted for vicarious-liability doctrine in harassment cases, not to redefine the substantive reach of § 703(a)(1). Line-drawing and overbreadth concerns can be handled through ordinary factual development and causation rather than a categorical heightened-harm gloss that risks narrowing Title VII’s protections in practice.

John Roberts.reasoning: Title VII makes it unlawful to “discriminate against any individual with respect to [her] compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), and that text does not impose a freestanding requirement that the plaintiff show a “materially significant employment disadvantage” beyond a discriminatory change in those terms or conditions. Requiring an additional heightened harm screen risks narrowing the statute beyond Congress’s language and invites inconsistent, judge-made thresholds across circuits, undermining institutional legitimacy and uniformity in federal law. Consistent with Meritor Sav. Bank v. Vinson, Title VII’s antidiscrimination provision reaches non-economic changes that alter workplace conditions, and Burlington Indus., Inc. v. Ellerth’s “tangible employment action” framework—developed for harassment vicarious-liability rules—should not be imported as the general definition of an actionable adverse action for § 2000e-2(a)(1) disparate-treatment claims. I would resolve the case narrowly by holding that a discriminatory transfer is actionable if it effects a disadvantageous change in the employee’s terms or conditions of employment, without demanding proof of a materially significant economic or status loss.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of Title VII makes it unlawful to “discriminate against any individual with respect to his compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment” because of a protected trait. 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1). A job transfer is a paradigmatic change in the “terms” or “conditions” of employment, and the statute does not add a freestanding requirement that the plaintiff also prove a “materially significant” disadvantage beyond showing discrimination with respect to those terms or conditions. Consistent with the ordinary meaning approach this Court has employed in statutory cases, see Bostock v. Clayton County, 140 S. Ct. 1731, 1738 (2020), and this Court’s recognition that “terms” of employment encompass the benefits and incidents of the employment relationship, Hishon v. King & Spalding, 467 U.S. 69, 74 (1984), the Eighth Circuit’s heightened harm rule improperly narrows the statute Congress enacted.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 2000e-2(a)(1) bars discrimination with respect to an employee’s “compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment,” and that language is most naturally read to require a showing that the challenged action imposed a real, objective change in the employment relationship, not merely a subjective sense of lost prestige. Reading “terms” and “conditions” to reach any lateral transfer without a materially significant disadvantage would federalize routine assignment disputes and invite substantial second-guessing of day-to-day management decisions, with serious practical consequences for public employers and law enforcement operations. Burlington Northern & Santa Fe Ry. Co. v. White, 548 U.S. 53 (2006), adopted a “materially adverse” standard in the retaliation context, and it would be anomalous to treat core discrimination claims as actionable based on lesser effects than the Court required for retaliation. While Morgan identified “denial of transfer” as a discrete act, 536 U.S. 101, 114 (2002), that does not eliminate the need to show that the transfer decision actually altered the employee’s employment terms or conditions in a materially meaningful way.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Title VII’s text makes it unlawful to discriminate with respect to an employee’s “compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), and that language does not impose an extra requirement that the plaintiff prove a “materially significant” employment disadvantage beyond the discriminatory change itself. A discriminatory transfer can plainly alter the “terms” and “conditions” of work—duties, schedule, safety, and day-to-day professional standing—even if pay and rank stay the same, and requiring a heightened harm showing would improperly narrow the statute and undermine protection for workers in vulnerable positions. Burlington N. & Santa Fe Ry. Co. v. White confirms that a “materially adverse” threshold was adopted for retaliation claims because § 2000e-3(a) is not limited to workplace “terms, conditions, or privileges,” whereas § 2000e-2(a)(1) is already tethered to employment and therefore does not justify importing White’s limiting standard into disparate-treatment discrimination. Because discriminatory transfers are the kind of discrete employment decisions Title VII targets, the Eighth Circuit’s additional “significant disadvantage” gloss is inconsistent with the statutory text and structure.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 2000e-2(a)(1) makes it unlawful to discriminate “with respect to … compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment,” and that text already supplies the limiting principle: the challenged action must affect a term, condition, or privilege of employment, not necessarily impose a further, judicially invented showing of “materially significant” economic harm. Burlington Northern & Santa Fe Ry. Co. v. White, 548 U.S. 53 (2006), adopted a “materially adverse” screen for retaliation precisely because § 2000e-3(a) is not textually confined to terms and conditions; importing that requirement into § 2000e-2(a)(1) would blur the statute’s distinct provisions and narrow Congress’s chosen language. A discriminatory transfer that changes job duties, responsibilities, schedule, or workplace status can alter the “terms” and “conditions” of employment even if pay and title stay the same, and the Eighth Circuit’s heightened disadvantage test risks excluding such textual injuries. Workability is preserved by requiring a concrete effect on terms/conditions (not trivial slights), but not demanding an extra showing of significant material disadvantage beyond what the statute already demands.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 2000e-2(a)(1) makes it unlawful to discriminate against an individual with respect to her “compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment,” and that text supplies the limiting principle: the plaintiff must show discrimination that affects a term or condition of employment, not an extra, judge-made requirement of a “materially significant” disadvantage. Importing a heightened “material adversity” standard from retaliation cases would disregard the statute’s distinct language, because the antiretaliation provision is not expressly confined to workplace “terms, conditions, or privileges,” a difference this Court emphasized in Burlington N. & Santa Fe Ry. Co. v. White, 548 U.S. 53, 63–68 (2006). Consistent with separation-of-powers principles, courts should apply the line Congress drew in §2000e-2(a)(1) rather than narrowing liability through an additional atextual hurdle. Whether the particular transfer here altered a “term” or “condition” is for application on remand, but Title VII does not require a showing of a materially significant employment disadvantage beyond that statutory element.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 703(a)(1) makes it unlawful to discriminate with respect to an employee’s “compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), and that text does not impose a freestanding requirement that the plaintiff show a “materially significant employment disadvantage” beyond a discriminatory change in terms or conditions. The City’s reliance on “tangible employment action” concepts drawn from Burlington Industries, Inc. v. Ellerth, 524 U.S. 742 (1998), is misplaced because Ellerth addressed vicarious liability and an affirmative defense in the hostile-work-environment context, not the scope of § 2000e-2(a)(1)’s substantive prohibition. Likewise, Burlington Northern & Santa Fe Ry. Co. v. White, 548 U.S. 53 (2006), imposed a “materially adverse” requirement for retaliation claims based on the different statutory language in Title VII’s anti-retaliation provision, not § 703(a)(1). A workable, precedent-consistent rule is that a discriminatory transfer is actionable when it meaningfully alters an employee’s terms or conditions of employment, without importing a heightened “significant harm” gloss that is not rooted in the statute.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Title VII makes it unlawful to “discriminate against any individual with respect to [her] compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment.” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1). That text does not impose an extra-statutory requirement that the plaintiff show a “materially significant employment disadvantage” beyond a discriminatory change in the terms or conditions of employment, and importing such a threshold would be methodologically inconsistent with a textualist approach. Burlington Industries, Inc. v. Ellerth defined “tangible employment action” for purposes of vicarious-liability doctrine in supervisor-harassment cases, not to narrow the substantive scope of § 2000e-2(a)(1), and Burlington Northern & Santa Fe Ry. Co. v. White’s “materially adverse” standard applies to Title VII’s separate anti-retaliation provision, not the discrimination provision. Given the statute’s broad language and this Court’s recognition that Title VII reaches more than purely economic harms, a discriminatory transfer altering work conditions can be actionable without a heightened material-disadvantage showing.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Title VII’s antidiscrimination provision makes it unlawful to discriminate with respect to an employee’s “compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), and that text already supplies the limiting principle—courts should not add an extra, atextual requirement that a plaintiff prove a “materially significant” disadvantage beyond a discriminatory change in those terms or conditions. Burlington Northern & Santa Fe Ry. Co. v. White, 548 U.S. 53 (2006), adopted a “materially adverse” screen for retaliation precisely because § 2000e-3(a) is not tethered to “terms, conditions, or privileges of employment,” so White’s rationale does not justify importing a heightened harm requirement into § 2000e-2(a)(1). A discriminatory transfer that changes the nature of an employee’s work, responsibilities, schedule, or workplace environment can alter “terms” and “conditions” even if pay and rank are unchanged, and requiring tangible economic loss would undermine procedural fairness and Title VII’s practical enforcement. Disputes about whether the challenged transfer in fact altered the plaintiff’s terms or conditions, and whether any asserted harms are attributable to the employer’s decision, are factual and causation questions—not a categorical bar at the threshold.
